scenes.heading: Venn diagrams and two-way tables
scenes.sub: Some people say yes to both. Where do they go?
scenes.say: Ask a class who plays soccer and who plays netball. Some play both, some play neither. How do you count everyone exactly once? Venn diagrams and two-way tables.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Two drawers for socks, a middle drawer for socks that fit both
scenes.science: Two circles overlap; the middle region is in both sets
scenes.breaks: A real sock sits in one drawer, but the overlap counts as part of BOTH circles.
scenes.say: Picture two drawers: one for striped socks and one for woolly socks. A striped woolly sock needs a little middle drawer that belongs to both. Plain socks go in a box outside. That is a Venn diagram: every item goes in exactly one place.

scenes.heading: Four regions
scenes.say: Here is a class of thirty. First the rectangle, then the two circles. Nine play only soccer, five play both, seven play only netball, and nine play neither. Soccer and netball is just the overlap, five. Soccer or netball is twenty-one, counting the middle once.
scenes.caption: Here is a class of 30. First the rectangle, then the two circles. 9 play only soccer, 5 play both, 7 play only netball, and 9 play neither. Soccer and netball is just the overlap, 5. Soccer or netball is 21, counting the middle once.

scenes.heading: Unknown overlap? Call it x
scenes.say: Forty students: twenty-two have a dog, seventeen a cat, and six have neither. Call the overlap x. Then dog only is twenty-two minus x, and cat only is seventeen minus x. All four regions add to forty, so forty-five minus x equals forty, and x is five.
scenes.caption: 40 students: 22 have a dog, 17 a cat, and 6 have neither. Call the overlap x. Then dog only is 22 − x, and cat only is 17 − x. All four regions add to 40, so 45 − x = 40, and x = 5.

scenes.heading: Two-way tables
points: Each cell matches one Venn region
Rows and columns add to their totals
scenes.say: A two-way table holds the same four numbers. Rows are A and not A, columns are B and not B, and there are totals on the edges. Every row and column must add up, which makes missing values easy to find.

scenes.heading: Who is in the hat?
scenes.question: Year 8 row: 8 bus, 13 walk, 21 total. A Year 8 student is chosen. P(walks)?
scenes.say: In one survey, Year 8 has eight bus riders and thirteen walkers, twenty-one in total. If a Year 8 student is chosen, only Year 8s are in the hat. So divide by twenty-one, not the whole survey. The answer is thirteen twenty-firsts.
scenes.caption: In one survey, Year 8 has 8 bus riders and 13 walkers, 21 in total. If a Year 8 student is chosen, only Year 8s are in the hat. So divide by 21, not the whole survey. The answer is 13/21.

points: Four regions add to the total
Divide by who could be chosen
scenes.say: Quick recap. The four regions add to the total. Fill in the middle first, then subtract. Or counts the overlap once. And for probability, divide by the people who could be chosen. Now try the practice questions!
